Castle
KAS-el
noun
From the Latin castellum, diminutive of castrum, “a fortified place or camp,” through Anglo-Saxon castel; in the Authorized Version it renders several words — a stronghold, a fortified tower, an encampment of tents, and the Roman barracks at Jerusalem.

Biblical Definition

The Authorized Version uses castle for any fortified holding, and the sense shifts with the setting. Among the sons of Ishmael it means fortified encampments — “by their towns, and by their castles; twelve princes according to their nations” (Gen 25:16). Of Jerusalem it means the Jebusite citadel that David took: “Nevertheless David took the castle of Zion, which is the city of David” (1Ch 11:5) — the stronghold that had been counted impregnable, seized and made the seat of the LORD’s anointed. In the Acts it is the Antonia, the Roman barracks overlooking the temple court, into which Paul was carried when the multitude would have torn him in pieces (Act 21:34; Act 23:10). There the apostle stood on the stairs and preached to the mob that had just tried to kill him, and there the Lord stood by him in the night and said, Be of good cheer. The military sense of the word underlies its great spiritual use. Israel knew what walls were for, and knew that walls fail: horses and chariots and high towers are a vain thing for safety. So Solomon sets the true fortress over against every stone one: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Pro 18:10). The believer’s castle is not a place but a Person, and the gate is never shut against him.

Webster 1828 Definition

A fortified building or stronghold; also a fortified encampment, and in the Acts the Roman barracks at Jerusalem into which Paul was taken.

CASTLE, a house fortified for defense against an enemy; a fortress.

From the Latin castellum, a diminutive of castrum, a fortified camp.

In Scripture, sometimes a walled encampment of a nomadic people (Gen 25:16).

The stronghold of Zion, taken by David from the Jebusites (1Ch 11:5).

In the Acts, the fortress adjoining the temple where the Roman garrison lay (Act 21:34).

Key Scripture

Gen 25:16 — "These are the sons of Ishmael, and these are their names, by their towns, and by their castles; twelve princes according to their nations."

1Ch 11:5 — "And the inhabitants of Jebus said to David, Thou shalt not come hither. Nevertheless David took the castle of Zion, which is the city of David."

Act 21:34 — "And some cried one thing, some another, among the multitude: and when he could not know the certainty for the tumult, he commanded him to be carried into the castle."

Act 23:10 — "And when there arose a great dissension, the chief captain, fearing lest Paul should have been pulled in pieces of them, commanded the soldiers to go down, and to take him by force from among them, and to bring him into the castle."

Modern Corruption

No postmodern redefinition attaches to the word; the live danger is the old one of trusting the wall instead of the LORD, and of mistaking a place of safety for the source of it.

expand to see more

The abiding temptation the word exposes is trust misplaced in defences. Judah looked to the armour of the house of the forest, to the waters of the lower pool, to the strength of walls, and did not look unto the maker thereof. Every age builds its castle and calls it security — a fortified savings, a fortified reputation, a fortified household, a fortified nation — and every castle in Scripture eventually falls to someone. Even the castle of Zion, taken by David and made the city of the great King, was afterwards broken down and burned when the people within it forsook the covenant. The wall is not wicked; the trust is. Nehemiah built walls and prayed; David took the stronghold and sang that the LORD was his rock and his fortress. The sin is not fortification but the quiet transfer of confidence from the LORD of hosts to the works of our hands.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the only impregnable stronghold in Scripture is a name. “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Pro 18:10) — and notice the two things required, that the man be righteous and that he run. The tower does not shelter those who admire it from a distance; it shelters those who flee into it, which is exactly what faith does with Christ. Notice also that Paul’s safest night in Jerusalem was spent as a prisoner inside a pagan garrison, because the Lord who stood by him was his real defence and used a Roman fortress as an instrument. God can make a castle of anything, or of nothing. The saints have been safest in dens and caves and have perished in citadels; the difference has never been the masonry.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin castellum from castrum, a fortified camp; behind the English lie Hebrew tirah (an encircled encampment), metsudah (a stronghold), and Greek parembolē (the barracks or camp).

expand to see more

Hebrew — tirah (טירה), an encampment ringed with stone or tents, rendered castles in Gen 25:16.

Hebrew — metsudah (מצודה), a stronghold or fastness; the castle of Zion in 1Ch 11:5, and the psalmist’s word for God Himself.

Hebrew — birah (בירה), a palace-fortress, used of the temple citadel in 1Ch 29:1 and of Shushan the palace.

Greek — parembolē (παρεμβολή), a camp or barracks; the Antonia fortress in Act 21–23.

Latin — castellum, diminutive of castrum; the same root gives English chester in place-names.

Usage

"“David took the castle of Zion, and the place men called impregnable became the city of the king.”"

"“Paul preached from the stairs of the castle to the very mob that had dragged him out of the temple.”"

"“A man may lose every wall he has built and still be safe, if he has run into the name of the LORD.”"
